turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Great question, and welcome to the rose world! I’ll keep this really simple.

1. Where the rose grows (shape & use)

Bush / shrub roses: Round, bushy plants. Great for flower beds and borders. Easiest place to start.
Climbing roses: Long canes that need support (trellis, fence, arch). They don’t cling on their own; you tie them in place.
Groundcover / landscape roses: Low and spreading, good for covering an area or spilling over walls.

2. How the flowers appear

Hybrid tea roses: Classic “long-stem” look. One big flower per stem, great for cutting and vases.
Floribunda roses: Lots of flowers in clusters. Slightly smaller blooms but many at once; very showy.
English/old-style roses: Very full, many-petaled flowers, often with strong fragrance and a romantic look.

3. Bloom habit (how often they flower)

Repeat/continuous bloomers: Flower, rest, then flower again through the season. Most people prefer these because you get color for months.
Once-blooming: One big show per year, usually in spring/early summer, then mostly just foliage.

4. Where you plan to plant them

In the ground: Best long-term option. Needs a sunny spot (roses like about 6 or more hours of direct sun).
In containers: Works well if you have a patio or balcony. You’ll use a larger pot and good quality potting soil.

5. Climate (hardiness zone)

Each rose variety is rated for certain temperature ranges (hardiness zones). On our site you can:
Choose your zone at the top of the page so you only see roses that like your climate.

What do beginners usually say about it in reviews?

Newer gardeners usually say a few consistent things in their reviews about their first Heirloom roses:

“It took off faster than I expected.”
People are often surprised how quickly the plant settles in, pushes new growth, and starts to size up, even when they planted later than ideal or in hot weather.

“It stayed healthy while I figured things out.”
Beginners often mention that the plant looks strong and “doesn’t skip a beat,” even if their watering or timing wasn’t perfect. That forgiving nature is a big confidence booster.

“I got blooms my first season.”
You’ll see a lot of comments along the lines of “already blooming” or “covered in flowers” within weeks or the first season, which helps people feel like they didn’t mess up.

“The color/flowers are even better than the photos.”
New growers often say the bloom color in person surprised them in a good way and that visitors comment on it.

“I’m new to roses and this made me want more.”
A common theme is, “I’m a beginner and now I’m hooked,” because a good first rose makes the whole process feel do‑able instead of fussy.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question, and good on you for wanting to start off right.

I’ll explain how to use the Get Growing Bundle the first time you plant your rose.

If you haven’t seen it already, this is the product we’ve been talking about: Get Growing Bundle

I’ll keep this to simple steps.

Before you start
This bundle has four parts:
Bone meal
Aged cow manure
Mint compost
Founders Fish Fertilizer
You’ll use the dry ingredients (bone meal, manure, compost) in the planting hole, and the Founders Fish as a gentle liquid feed after planting.
Prepare the planting hole (for planting in the ground)
Dig a hole about 2 feet wide and deep enough that the rose will sit at the same level it was in its pot.
Set the native soil to the side in a pile.
Add the dry amendments
In the bottom of the hole:
Put a layer of aged cow manure (just a few inches deep; enough to lightly cover the bottom).
In your soil pile:
Mix some of the bone meal into the soil you removed.
Mix in mint compost until that soil looks rich and crumbly (roughly 1 part compost to 2 parts native soil is a good, easy rule of thumb).
Plant the rose
Put some of the amended soil (with bone meal + compost) on top of the manure layer.
Set the rose in the hole so the base of the plant is at soil level.
Backfill around the roots with the amended soil, pressing gently so there are no big air pockets.
Water well with plain water to settle everything.
Use Founders Fish Fertilizer
Mix Founders Fish Fertilizer in water according to the directions on the bottle label (follow their ratio; that is important so it stays gentle).
After the first good plain watering, give the plant a drink of the mixed fish fertilizer over the root zone.
After that, you can repeat the fish fertilizer every 4 weeks during the growing season to support steady growth.
If you are planting in a container instead
Fill the pot with a good-quality potting soil (not garden soil).
Mix a small amount of bone meal and mint compost into that potting soil before planting.
Do not put a thick layer of pure manure at the very bottom of a container (it can get too soggy). Instead, mix a little into the potting mix if you want to use it.
Plant the rose, water well, then use the Founders Fish Fertilizer mix as above.
